source_text: Ἀνάγει γοῦν ὁ τοιοῦτος φόβος ἐπί τε τὴν μετάνοιαν ἐπί τε τὴν ἐλπίδα. ἐλπὶς δὲ προσδοκία ἀγαθῶν ἡ ἀπόντος ἀγαθοῦ εὔελπις. ἀμέλει καὶ ἡ εὐεμπτωσία λαμβάνεται εἰς ἐλπίδα, ἣν ἐπὶ τὴν ἀγάπην χειραγωγεῖν μεμαθήκαμεν. ἀγάπη δὲ ὁμόνοια ἂν εἴη τῶν κατὰ τὸν λόγον καὶ τὸν βίον καὶ τὸν τρόπον ἢ συνελόντι φάναι κοινωνία βίου ἢ ἐκτένεια φιλίας καὶ φιλοστοργίας μετὰ λόγου ὀρθοῦ περὶ χρῆσιν ἑταίρω. ὁ δὲ ἑταῖρος ἕτερος ἐγώ· ᾗ καὶ ἀδελφοὺς τοὺς τῷ αὐτῷ λόγῳ ἀναγεννηθέντας προσαγορεύομεν. παράκειται δὲ τῇ ἀγάπῃ ἥ τε φιλοξενία, φιλοτεχνία τις οὖσα περὶ χρῆσιν ξένων· ξένοι δὲ ὧν ξένα τὰ κοσμικά. κοσμικοὺς γὰρ τοὺς εἰς γῆν ἐλπίζοντας καὶ τὰς σαρκικὰς ἐπιθυμίας ἐξακούομεν· μὴ συσχηματίζεσθε, φησὶν ὁ ἀπόστολος, τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ, ἀλλὰ μεταμορφοῦσθε τῇ ἀνακαινώσει τοῦ νοός, εἰς τὸ δοκιμάζειν ὑμᾶς τί τὸ θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ, τὸ ἀγαθὸν καὶ εὐάρεστον καὶ τέλειον. ἀναστρέφει τοίνυν ἡ φιλοξενία περὶ τὸ ὠφέλιμον τοῖς ξένοις, ξένοι δὲ οἱ ἐπίξενοι, ἐπίξενοι δὲ οἱ φίλοι, φίλοι δὲ οἱ ἀδελφοί· φίλε κασίγνητε φησὶν Ὅμηρος, ἥ τε φιλανθρωπία, δἰ ἣν καὶ ἡ φιλοστοργία, φιλικὴ χρῆσις ἀνθρώπων ὑπάρχουσα, ἥ τε φιλοστοργία, φιλοτεχνία τις οὖσα περὶ στέρξιν φίλων ἢ οἰκείων, συμπαρομαρτοῦσιν ἀγάπῃ. εἰ δ’ ὁ τῷ ὄντι ἄνθρωπος ὁ ἐν ἡμῖν ἐστιν ὁ πνευματικός, φιλαδελφία ἡ φιλανθρωπία τοῖς τοῦ αὐτοῦ πνεύματος κεκοινωνηκόσιν· στέρξις δ’ αὖ τήρησίς ἐστιν εὐνοίας ἢ ἀγαπήσεως, ἀγάπησις δὲ ἀπόδεξις παντελής, καὶ τὸ ἀγαπᾶν ἀρέσκεσθαι τῷ ἤδει, ἀγόμενόν τε καὶ ἀπαγόμενον· ἄγονται δὲ εἰς ταὐτότητα δἰ ὁμόνοιαν, ἐπιστήμην οὖσαν κοινῶν ἀγαθῶν· καὶ γὰρ ἡ ὁμογνωμοσύνη συμφωνία γνωμῶν. καὶ ἡ ἀγάπη φησὶν ἀνυπόκριτος ἔστω ἡμῖν, αὐτοί τε ἀποστυγοῦντες τὸ πονηρὸν γινώμεθα, κολλώμενοι τῷ ἀγαθῷ τῇ φιλαδελφίᾳ τε καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς ἕως εἰ δυνατόν, τὸ ἐξ ὑμῶν, μετὰ πάντων ἀνθρώπων εἰρηνεύοντες. ἔπειτα μὴ νικῶ λέγει ὑπὸ τοῦ κακοῦ, ἀλλὰ νίκα ἐν τῷ ἀγαθῷ τὸ κακόν. Ἰουδαίοις τε ὁ αὐτὸς ἀπόστολος μαρτυρεῖν ὁμολογεῖ ὅτι ζῆλον θεοῦ ἔχουσιν, ἀλλ’ οὐ κατ’ ἐπίγνωσιν· ἀγνοοῦντες γὰρ τὴν τοῦ θεοῦ δικαιοσύνην, καὶ τὴν ἰδίαν ζητοῦντες στῆσαι, τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ τοῦ θεοῦ οὐχ ὑπετάγησαν· οὐ γὰρ τὸ βούλημα τοῦ νόμου ἔγνωσάν τε καὶ ἐποίησαν, ἀλλ’ ὃ ὑπέλαβον αὐτοί, τοῦτο καὶ βούλεσθαι τὸν νόμον ᾠήθησαν· οὐδ’ ὡς προφητεύοντι τῷ νόμῳ ἐπίστευσαν, λόγῳ δὲ ψιλῷ καὶ φόβῳ, ἀλλ’ οὐ διαθέσει καὶ πίστει ἠκολούθησαν· τέλος γὰρ νόμου Χριστὸς εἰς δικαιοσύνην, ὁ ὑπὸ νόμου προφητευθείς, παντὶ τῷ πιστεύοντι. ὅθεν εἴρηται τούτοις παρὰ Μωυσέως· ἐγὼ παραζηλώσω ὑμᾶς ἐπ’ οὐκ ἔθνει, ἐπ’ ἔθνει ἀσυνέτῳ παροργιῶ ὑμᾶς, τῷ εἰς ὑπακοὴν δηλονότι εὐτρεπεῖ γενομένῳ. καὶ διὰ Ἡσαΐου εὑρέθην λέγει τοῖς ἐμὲ μὴ ζητοῦσιν, ἐμφανὴς ἐγενόμην τοῖς ἐμὲ μὴ ἐπερωτῶσι, πρὸ τῆς τοῦ κυρίου παρουσίας δηλαδή, μεθ’ ἣν καὶ τῷ Ἰσραὴλ ἐκεῖνα τὰ προφητευθέντα οἰκείως λέγεται νῦν· ἐξεπέτασα τὰς χεῖράς μου ὅλην τὴν ἡμέραν ἐπὶ λαὸν ἀπειθοῦντα καὶ ἀντιλέγοντα. ὁρᾷς τὴν αἰτίαν τῆς ἐξ ἐθνῶν κλήσεως σαφῶς πρὸς τοῦ προφήτου ἀπείθειαν τοῦ λαοῦ καὶ ἀντιλογίαν εἰρημένην; εἶθ’ ἡ ἀγαθότης καὶ ἐπὶ τούτοις δείκνυται τοῦ θεοῦ· φησὶ γὰρ ὁ ἀπόστολος· ἀλλὰ τῷ αὐτῶν παραπτώματι ἡ σωτηρία τοῖς ἔθνεσιν εἰς τὸ παραζηλῶσαι αὐτοὺς καὶ μετανοῆσαι βουληθῆναι. ὁ Ποιμὴν δὲ ἁπλῶς ἐπὶ τῶν κεκοιμημένων θεὶς τὴν λέξιν δικαίους οἶδέ τινας ἐν ἔθνεσι καὶ ἐν Ἰουδαίοις οὐ μόνον πρὸ τῆς τοῦ κυρίου παρουσίας, ἀλλὰ καὶ πρὸ νόμου κατὰ τὴν πρὸς θεὸν εὐαρέστησιν, ὡς Ἄβελ, ὡς Νῶε, ὡς εἴ τις ἕτερος δίκαιος. φησὶ γοῦν τοὺς ἀποστόλους καὶ διδασκάλους τοὺς κηρύξαντας τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ κοιμηθέντας τῇ δυνάμει καὶ τῇ πίστει κηρῦξαι τοῖς προκεκοιμημένοις. εἶτα ἐπιφέρει· καὶ αὐτοὶ ἔδωκαν αὐτοῖς τὴν σφραγῖδα τοῦ κηρύγματος. κατέβησαν οὖν μετ’ αὐτῶν εἰς τὸ ὕδωρ καὶ πάλιν ἀνέβησαν. ἀλλ’ οὗτοι ζῶντες κατέβησαν καὶ πάλιν ζῶντες ἀνέβησαν· ἐκεῖνοι δὲ οἱ προκεκοιμημένοι νεκροὶ κατέβησαν, ζῶντες δὲ ἀνέβησαν, διὰ τούτων οὖν ἐζωοποιήθησαν καὶ ἐπέγνωσαν τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ. διὰ τοῦτο καὶ συνανέβησαν μετ’ αὐτῶν καὶ συνήρμοσαν εἰς τὴν οἰκοδομὴν τοῦ πύργου καὶ ἀλατόμητοι συνῳκοδομήθησαν· ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ γὰρ ἐκοιμήθησαν καὶ ἐν μεγάλῃ ἁγνείᾳ, μόνην δὲ τὴν σφραγῖδα ταύτην οὐκ ἔσχον. ὅταν γὰρ ἔθνη τὰ μὴ νόμον ἔχοντα φύσει τὰ τοῦ νόμου ποιῶσιν, οὗτοι νόμον μὴ ἔχοντες ἑαυτοῖς εἰσι νόμος κατὰ τὸν ἀπόστολον. Ὡς μὲν οὖν ἀντακολουθοῦσιν ἀλλήλαις αἱ ἀρεταί, τί χρὴ λέγειν, ἐπιδεδειγμένου ἤδη ὡς πίστις μὲν ἐπὶ μετανοίᾳ ἐλπίδι τε, εὐλάβεια δὲ ἐπὶ πίστει, καὶ ἡ ἐν τούτοις ἐπιμονή τε καὶ ἄσκησις ἅμα μαθήσει συμπεραιοῦται εἰς ἀγάπην, ἣ δὲ τῇ γνώσει τελειοῦται; ἐκεῖνο δὲ ἐξ ἀνάγκης παρασημειωτέον ὡς μόνον τὸ θεῖον σοφὸν εἶναι φύσει νοεῖσθαι χρή· διὸ καὶ ἡ σοφία δύναμις θεοῦ ἡ διδάξασα τὴν ἀλήθειαν· κἀνταῦθά που εἴληπται ἡ τελείωσις τῆς γνώσεως. φιλεῖ δὲ καὶ ἀγαπᾷ τὴν ἀλήθειαν ὁ φιλόσοφος, ἐκ τοῦ θεράπων εἶναι γνήσιος δἰ ἀγάπην ἤδη φίλος νομισθείς. ταύτης δὲ ἀρχὴ τὸ θαυμάσαι τὰ πράγματα, ὡς Πλάτων ἐν Θεαιτήτῳ λέγει, καὶ Ματθίας ἐν ταῖς Παραδόσεσι παραινῶν θαύμασον τὰ παρόντα, βαθμὸν τοῦτον πρῶτον τῆς ἐπέκεινα γνώσεως ὑποτιθέμενος· ᾗ κἀν τῷ καθ’ Ἑβραίους εὐαγγελίῳ ὁ θαυμάσας βασιλεύσει γέγραπται καὶ ὁ βασιλεύσας ἀναπαήσεται. ἀδύνατον οὖν τὸν ἀμαθῆ, ἔστ’ ἂν μένῃ ἀμαθής, φιλοσοφεῖν δέ, τόν γε μὴ ἔννοιαν σοφίας εἰληφότα, φιλοσοφίας οὔσης ὀρέξεως τοῦ ὄντως ὄντος καὶ τῶν εἰς τοῦτο συντεινόντων μαθημάτων. κἂν τὸ ποιεῖν καλῶς ᾖ τισιν ἐξησκημένον, ἀλλὰ τὸ ἐπίστασθαι, ὡς χρηστέον καὶ ποιητέον, καὶ συνεκπονητέον, καθὸ καὶ ὁμοιοῦταί τις θεῷ, θεῷ λέγω τῷ σωτῆρι, θεραπεύων τὸν τῶν ὅλων θεὸν διὰ τοῦ ἀρχιερέως λόγου, δἰ οὗ καθορᾶται τὰ κατ’ ἀλήθειαν καλὰ καὶ δίκαια. εὐσέβεια ἔστι πρᾶξις ἑπομένη καὶ ἀκόλουθος θεῷ.
pass_a_gloss: For such fear leads to repentance and to hope. Hope is the expectation of good things, the expectation of the good that is absent, with good expectations. And so even gentleness is taken into hope, which we have learned to lead to love. Love is harmony of those according to the word and the life and the manner, or to say it briefly, community of life or longing of friendship and affection with right word about the use of friends. The friend is another I; for this reason we also address as brothers those who have been reborn in the same word. Hospitality is placed beside love, a kind of affection about the use of strangers; strangers are those for whom the worldly things are strange. For we hear that the worldly ones are those who hope in the earth and the fleshly desires; do not be conformed, the apostle says, to this age, but be transformed by the renewal of the mind, so that you may discern what is the will of God, the good and pleasing and perfect. Therefore hospitality turns to what is beneficial for strangers, strangers are those who are foreign, foreign are those who are friends, friends are those who are brothers; dear brother, as Homer says. And also philanthropy, through which also affection, a friendly use of people exists, and also affection, a kind of affection about the love of friends or relatives, run together with love. If the true human being in us is the spiritual one, philanthropy is love of brothers to those who have shared in the same spirit. Affection is the keeping of good will or love, and love is a complete acceptance, and to love is to be pleased with the good, being led and leading. They are led to the same thing through harmony, which is knowledge of common goods; for also like-mindedness is harmony of minds. And love, the apostle says, let it be without hypocrisy; let us also know ourselves, hating the evil and clinging to the good with love of brothers and the following things, as far as possible, being at peace with all people. Then do not be overcome, he says, by evil, but overcome evil with good. The apostle also testifies to the Jews that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge; for being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to the righteousness of God; for they did not know the will of the law, nor did they do it, but they thought that the law wills what they themselves will; nor did they believe in the law as prophesying, but with empty word and fear, and not with disposition and faith they followed. For the end of the law is Christ, for righteousness to everyone who believes, the one prophesied under the law. Therefore it has been said to them by Moses: I will provoke you to jealousy on account of those who are not a nation, on a nation without understanding I will provoke you, clearly to obedience. And through Isaiah it is said to those who do not seek me, I was found by those who did not ask for me, before the coming of the Lord, after which also to Israel those things that were prophesied are said to belong; I stretched out my hands all day to a disobedient and contradicting people. Do you see the reason for the calling of the nations, clearly stated by the prophet, because of the disobedience and contradiction of the people? Then the goodness of God is also shown to them; for the apostle says: but salvation to the nations is due to their transgression, so that they may be provoked to jealousy and repentance. The Shepherd, having placed the word on the righteous who have fallen asleep, knows that there are some righteous ones among the nations and among the Jews, not only before the coming of the Lord, but also before the law, according to the pleasing to God, as Abel, as Noah, as anyone else righteous. For he says that the apostles and teachers, who preached the name of the Son of God and fell asleep with power and faith, preached to those who had fallen asleep before. Then he adds: and they themselves gave them the seal of the preaching. They went down with them into the water and came up again. But these, being alive, went down and came up again alive; those who had fallen asleep, having died, went down, but came up alive, and through these they were made alive and came to know the name of the Son of God. For this reason they also rose together with them and were joined to the building of the tower and were built together unharmed; for they fell asleep in righteousness and in great purity, but they did not have this one seal alone. For when nations that do not have the law do by nature the things of the law, these, not having the law, are a law to themselves, according to the apostle. As virtues follow one another, what need is there to say, since it has already been shown that faith is on repentance and hope, and reverence is on faith, and the perseverance and practice in these things, along with learning, lead together to love, which is perfected by knowledge? But it must be noted that only the divine is wise by nature, and therefore wisdom is the power of God, which teaches the truth; and perhaps the perfection of knowledge is taken from there. The philosopher also loves and cherishes the truth, being a true servant through love, and is considered a friend. The beginning of this is to marvel at things, as Plato says in the Theaetetus, and Matthias in the Traditions, advising to marvel at what is present, considering this as the first step of the knowledge that is beyond. In which also in the Hebrew gospel it is written that the one who marvels will reign and the one who reigns will rest. It is impossible for the unlearned, as long as they remain unlearned, to philosophize, I mean the one who has not received the notion of wisdom, since philosophy is a desire for what truly exists and the lessons that lead to it. And even if doing good is practiced by some, but not knowing how to use and do and cooperate, as one becomes like God, I say God the Savior, serving the God of all things through the word of the high priest, through which the true good and just things are seen. Piety is a practice that follows and accompanies God.

pass_b_english: Fear of this kind leads both to repentance and to hope. Hope is the expectation of good things — the expectation of a good that is absent but anticipated. Even gentleness is drawn into hope, which we have learned to guide toward love. Love is the harmony of those who live by the word, the life, and the manner; to put it concisely, it is a community of life, a longing of friendship and natural affection, governed by right reason about how we treat our friends. A friend is another self; therefore we call brothers those who have been reborn through the same word. Hospitality stands beside love, a kind of skill in caring for strangers. Strangers are those for whom worldly things are alien. Worldly people, the apostle says, are those who set their hope on the earth and obey fleshly desires; "do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, so that you may discern what is the will of God — what is good, pleasing, and perfect" (Romans 12:2). Thus hospitality turns toward what benefits strangers; strangers are foreigners, foreigners are friends, friends are brothers — "dear brother," as Homer says. Philanthropy also accompanies love, for through it natural affection arises, a friendly use of people; and natural affection, a skill in caring for friends or relatives, runs together with love. If the true human being within us is the spiritual one, then philanthropy becomes love of brothers toward those who share the same Spirit. Affection is the keeping of goodwill or love; love is complete acceptance; to love is to delight in the good, both leading and being led. We are led into unity through harmony, which is the knowledge of common goods; for like‑mindedness is harmony of minds. And love, the apostle says, "let it be without hypocrisy; let us know ourselves, hating the evil and clinging to the good with brotherly love and the virtues that follow, as far as possible, living at peace with all people" (cf. Romans 12:9–18). Then "do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good" (cf. Romans 12:21). The same apostle testifies to the Jews that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge; for being ignorant of God's righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God's righteousness. They did not know the will of the law, nor did they do it; they thought the law willed whatever they themselves willed. Nor did they believe the law as prophesying, but followed it with empty words and fear, not with disposition and faith. "For the end of the law is Christ, for righteousness to everyone who believes," the one prophesied under the law (Romans 10:4). Therefore it was said to them by Moses: "I will provoke you to jealousy by those who are not a nation; by a nation without understanding I will anger you" (Deuteronomy 32:21), plainly to obedience. And through Isaiah: "I was found by those who did not seek me; I revealed myself to those who did not ask for me" (Isaiah 65:1), before the coming of the Lord, after which those things prophesied to Israel are now said to belong to it fittingly: "I stretched out my hands all day to a disobedient and contrary people." Do you see the reason for the calling of the nations, clearly stated by the prophet, because of the people's disobedience and contradiction? Then the goodness of God is also shown to them; for the apostle says: "but through their transgression salvation has come to the nations, to provoke them to jealousy and to repentance" (cf. Romans 11:11). The Shepherd, placing the word on the righteous who have fallen asleep, knows that there are some righteous ones among the nations and among the Jews — not only before the coming of the Lord, but also before the law, according to what pleases God, like Abel, like Noah, and any other righteous person. He says that the apostles and teachers who preached the name of the Son of God and fell asleep in power and faith also preached to those who had fallen asleep before. Then he adds: "and they themselves gave them the seal of the preaching." They went down with them into the water and came up again. But these, being alive, went down and came up alive; those who had fallen asleep, having died, went down, but came up alive, and through this they were made alive and came to know the name of the Son of God. For this reason they also rose together with them and were joined to the building of the tower, fitted together unharmed; for they fell asleep in righteousness and great purity, yet they lacked this one seal alone. For when nations that do not have the law do by nature the things of the law, these, though they have no law, are a law to themselves, according to the apostle (cf. Romans 2:14). Since virtues follow one another, what need is there to say more, now that it has been shown that faith follows repentance and hope, reverence follows faith, and perseverance and practice in these, together with learning, lead together to love, which is perfected by knowledge? But it must be noted that only the divine is wise by nature; therefore wisdom is the power of God, which teaches the truth; and perhaps the perfection of knowledge is taken from there. The philosopher loves and cherishes the truth, becoming a true servant through love and counted a friend. The beginning of this is to marvel at things, as Plato says in the Theaetetus, and Matthias in the Traditions, urging us to marvel at what is present, treating this as the first step toward the knowledge that lies beyond. In which also in the Hebrew gospel it is written: "the one who marvels will reign, and the one who reigns will rest." It is impossible for the unlearned, as long as they remain unlearned, to philosophize — I mean the one who has not received the notion of wisdom, since philosophy is a desire for what truly exists and the lessons that lead to it. Even if doing good is practiced by some, the knowing how to use and do and cooperate, so that one becomes like God — I say God the Savior — serving the God of all things through the word of the high priest, through which the truly good and just things are seen (Hebrews 13:15). Piety is a practice that follows and accompanies God.

review.notes: Checked all clauses in paragraph 1. Pass A and B both accurately reflect the Greek. Scripture citations in Pass B are correctly identified and added (Romans 12:2, Romans 12:9-18, Romans 12:21, Romans 10:4, Deuteronomy 32:21, Isaiah 65:1, Romans 11:11, Romans 2:14, Hebrews 13:15). The translation of 'φιλοστοργία' as 'natural affection' or 'affection' is consistent. The translation of 'φιλοτεχνία' as 'skill' or 'kind of affection' is acceptable. The title 'Fear and Hope' captures the opening thought.
